note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

UN9.title: Goal 9: Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation
UN9.publisher: United Nations Department of Global Communications

questions.prompt: What share of the world's population has NO access to a mobile broadband network at all?
questions.whyCorrect: 4% — around 300 million people live outside the reach of any mobile network. Not too poor for a phone: there is simply no signal where they live.
whyWrong: Ten times too high — coverage is now almost universal.
A small share still lives beyond any signal.
questions.action: Find the last place you visited with no bars of signal.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's population is covered by a 4G network?
questions.whyCorrect: 92%. 4G went from a luxury to near-universal coverage in about fifteen years — one of the fastest technology rollouts in history.
whyWrong: That's the 4G figure for low-income countries.
Far too low — 4G is nearly everywhere.
questions.action: Ask an adult what phones could do before 4G.

questions.prompt: 5G now covers what share of the world's population?
questions.whyCorrect: 51% — just over half the world, only a few years after launch. But covered is not the same as connected or affordable.
whyWrong: Far too low — 5G passed half the world.
That's closer to 4G coverage.
questions.action: Check whether your area has 5G.

questions.prompt: In low-income countries, 5G covers what share of people?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 4%, against 51% globally. The newest technology arrives in rich places first and poor places last — sometimes decades later.
whyWrong: That's the global figure, not the low-income one.
Far too optimistic for low-income countries.
questions.action: Compare 4% with the global 51%.

questions.prompt: In low-income countries, 4G covers what share of people?
questions.whyCorrect: 52% — barely half, against 92% worldwide. Almost one in two people there cannot get the network the rest of the world takes for granted.
whyWrong: That's the global figure.
Too pessimistic — about half are covered.
questions.action: Ask what you could not do today with no mobile data.

questions.prompt: How many researchers does the world have per million people?
questions.whyCorrect: 1,420 per million — about one researcher for every 700 people, up from 1,137 in 2015.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Work out how many researchers your town would have.

questions.prompt: Sub-Saharan Africa has how many researchers per million people?
questions.whyCorrect: 91 per million — against 4,254 in Europe and North America. That is a 47-fold gap in who gets to do science.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
That's the world average.
questions.action: Ask what a country loses when it cannot train scientists.

questions.prompt: Europe and Northern America have how many researchers per million?
questions.whyCorrect: 4,254 — three times the world average and 47 times sub-Saharan Africa's 91. Discovery is concentrated in a few countries.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
Ten times too low — below even the world average.
questions.action: Name three inventions and find out where they were made.

questions.prompt: How much of the world's income goes into research and development?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.95% of global GDP — under one dollar in fifty. It's risen from 1.72% in 2015, but nearly all the growth is in already-rich economies.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
Far too low — R&D is a real slice of the economy.
questions.action: Ask why companies hesitate to spend on research.

questions.prompt: What share of small manufacturing businesses worldwide can get a loan or credit line?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 31%. More than two in three small factories cannot borrow to buy a machine, hire staff or take an order — the single biggest brake on small industry.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic — most small firms are locked out.
Too pessimistic — about a third do have credit.
questions.action: Ask what a small business needs money for before it earns any.

questions.prompt: In sub-Saharan Africa, what share of small manufacturers can get credit?
questions.whyCorrect: 18% — the lowest of any region, against 46% in Latin America and the Caribbean. Where capital is scarcest, it is also hardest to borrow.
whyWrong: That's the Latin American figure.
That's the global average.
questions.action: Ask why banks judge some borrowers riskier than others.

questions.prompt: Latin America and the Caribbean lead the world on small-business credit, at:
questions.whyCorrect: 46% — the highest regional figure, and still under half. Even the best-performing region leaves most small manufacturers unbanked.
whyWrong: That's closer to sub-Saharan Africa's 18%.
Far too optimistic — no region is near this.
questions.action: Ask what would change if every small firm could borrow.

questions.prompt: Global CO2 emissions in 2024 reached:
questions.whyCorrect: 37.6 gigatons — the highest ever recorded, 8.3% above 2015. Despite every climate pledge, industrial emissions are still going up.
whyWrong: Emissions are enormous and still rising.
Emissions hit a record high, not a low.
questions.action: Ask what has to change for emissions to fall, not just slow.

questions.prompt: How much did CO2 emissions rise between 2015 and 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: Up 8.3% — the years since the SDGs were agreed have seen emissions grow, not shrink.
whyWrong: Emissions rose over this period.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Find out what year your country's emissions peaked.

questions.prompt: How much CO2 did clean energy prevent between 2019 and 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 2.6 gigatons avoided — real and large, yet emissions still hit a record. Clean energy is growing fast but demand is growing faster.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
Clean energy has measurably reduced emissions.
questions.action: Ask why cleaner energy hasn't yet meant lower emissions.

questions.prompt: Manufacturing value added per person grew how much between 2015 and 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 17.3% — from $1,649 to $1,934 per person. The world genuinely makes more per head than it did a decade ago.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: List five things near you that were manufactured.

questions.prompt: Which region grew its manufacturing per person fastest since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Central and Southern Asia, up 42.1% — far ahead of the 17.3% world average. India and its neighbours are the engine room of new manufacturing.
whyWrong: Sub-Saharan Africa's manufacturing per person actually fell.
Australia and New Zealand's fell 10.5%.
questions.action: Check the country of origin labels on your clothes.

questions.prompt: Sub-Saharan Africa's manufacturing per person since 2015 has:
questions.whyCorrect: Fallen 5.9%. The region with the fastest-growing population is producing less per head than a decade ago — the opposite of industrialisation.
whyWrong: That's Central and Southern Asia.
There was a measurable decline.
questions.action: Ask what a country needs before factories will open there.

questions.prompt: Which of these regions saw manufacturing per person FALL since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Latin America and the Caribbean, down 8.0% — along with sub-Saharan Africa (−5.9%) and Australia and New Zealand (−10.5%). Growth is not universal.
whyWrong: It grew 42.1% — the fastest anywhere.
Three regions went backwards.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a town when its factory closes.

questions.prompt: In the least developed countries, manufacturing per person since 2015 has:
questions.whyCorrect: Grown 40.6% — better than the world average of 17.3%. The poorest countries are industrialising fast, from a very low base.
whyWrong: The trend in LDCs is strongly positive.
There has been substantial growth.
questions.action: Ask why growth looks big when the starting point is small.

questions.prompt: Manufacturing makes up what share of the world's total economy?
questions.whyCorrect: 16.5% — steady across 2023 and 2024. Most of the world economy is services, not making things.
whyWrong: Far too high — services dominate the world economy.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Sort ten jobs you know into making things and providing services.

questions.prompt: How much cargo moved by sea in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 11.6 billion tons — up from 6.2 billion in 2000. Roughly 80% of everything traded travels by ship.
whyWrong: A thousand times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Find out how your favourite snack reached your shop.

questions.prompt: Sea cargo in 2000 was 6.2 billion tons. By 2023 it was:
questions.whyCorrect: 11.6 billion tons — nearly doubled in a generation. Global trade grew faster than the global economy.
whyWrong: Sea trade nearly doubled.
It grew sharply, it did not shrink.
questions.action: Look up how many containers the biggest ship carries.

questions.prompt: Developing countries handled what share of the world's sea freight in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 54% — a majority, up from 38% in 2000. The centre of gravity of world trade has genuinely shifted.
whyWrong: Too high — it is just over half.
Far too low — developing countries now handle most of it.
questions.action: Find the world's busiest port and see which country it's in.

questions.prompt: Developing countries' share of sea freight in 2000 was 38%. In 2023 it was:
questions.whyCorrect: 54% — a 16-point rise in 23 years. Developing economies went from a third of world shipping to more than half.
whyWrong: The share rose, it did not fall.
It changed substantially.
questions.action: Ask what a country gains from a big port.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's workers have manufacturing jobs?
questions.whyCorrect: 13.7% — and falling, from 14.3% in 2015. Factories make more than ever with fewer workers, because machines do more of the work.
whyWrong: Too low — factory work is still a substantial share.
Far too high — most jobs are in services.
questions.action: Ask what jobs a modern factory still needs people for.

questions.prompt: Manufacturing employment's share of world jobs since 2015 has:
questions.whyCorrect: Fallen from 14.3% to 13.7%. Output is up and jobs are down — the definition of automation.
whyWrong: The share has been drifting down.
Nothing close to doubling.
questions.action: Ask which jobs near you a machine could not do.

questions.prompt: What share of the world lives within reach of a mobile broadband network?
questions.whyCorrect: 96%. Reaching the final 4% is the hard part — remote, sparse and unprofitable to serve.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — coverage is near-universal.
About 4% still have no coverage.
questions.action: Ask why the last 4% costs the most to reach.

questions.prompt: The world has 1,420 researchers per million people. In 2015 it had:
questions.whyCorrect: 1,137 — so research capacity has been growing about 4.3% a year. More people are doing science than at any point in history.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Researcher numbers rose, so 2015 was lower.
questions.action: Ask what a researcher actually does all day.

questions.prompt: R&D spending was 1.72% of world GDP in 2015. By 2022 it was:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.95% — a real rise, but still under one dollar in fifty, and heavily concentrated in a handful of countries.
whyWrong: R&D spending rose, it did not fall.
Far too high — no region spends this much.
questions.action: Ask what problem you'd fund research into first.

questions.prompt: The gap in researchers per million between Europe/North America and sub-Saharan Africa is about:
questions.whyCorrect: About 47 times — 4,254 against 91 per million. This is one of the widest gaps in any SDG indicator.
whyWrong: Vastly understates the gap.
The gap is enormous.
questions.action: Ask what it takes to become a researcher where you live.

questions.prompt: Global CO2 emissions rose how much from 2023 to 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 0.8% — the slowest growth in years, but still growth. Emissions must fall steeply, not merely rise slowly.
whyWrong: Emissions rose to a record high.
Ten times too high for a single year.
questions.action: Ask what the difference is between slowing and reversing.

questions.prompt: Manufacturing value added per person worldwide is now about:
questions.whyCorrect: $1,934 a year for every person on Earth, up from $1,649 in 2015. That is the value of everything manufactured, divided by everyone.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Estimate the value of the manufactured goods in your bag.

questions.prompt: Which region's manufacturing per person fell the MOST since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: Australia and New Zealand, down 10.5% — a bigger fall than sub-Saharan Africa's 5.9% or Latin America's 8.0%. Rich countries can de-industrialise too.
whyWrong: It fell 5.9% — a smaller decline.
It fell 8.0% — still less than Australia and New Zealand.
questions.action: Ask why a wealthy country might make fewer things over time.

questions.prompt: Global manufacturing growth in 2021 was 7.4%. In 2022 it was:
questions.whyCorrect: 2.7% — growth fell to about a third of the previous year as the post-pandemic rebound faded.
whyWrong: Growth slowed sharply, it did not accelerate.
That's the 2021 figure.
questions.action: Ask what makes factory output swing year to year.

questions.prompt: Two in three small manufacturers cannot get credit. The main consequence is:
options: They cannot grow or buy equipment
questions.whyCorrect: Without credit a small firm cannot buy a machine, hire ahead of an order, or survive a slow month — so it stays small forever.
whyWrong: Credit access is unrelated to tax bills.
Lack of credit makes exporting harder, not easier.
questions.action: Ask a local shop owner what they'd buy with a loan.

questions.prompt: Being covered by a 5G network means you:
options: Could use it if you had a phone and could afford data
questions.whyCorrect: Coverage only means the signal reaches you. A device and affordable data are separate barriers — which is why usage lags far behind coverage.
whyWrong: Coverage and actual use are very different numbers.
Networks are not free to use.
questions.action: Work out the monthly cost of data where you live.

questions.prompt: Which is closest to the number of people with no mobile network at all?
questions.whyCorrect: About 300 million — 4% of humanity, mostly in remote rural areas where building a mast costs more than it earns.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too high.
questions.action: Find the most remote inhabited place you can on a map.

questions.prompt: Infrastructure means:
options: The shared systems everything else runs on — roads, power, water, networks, ports
questions.whyCorrect: Infrastructure is the shared foundation: without power, roads, water and networks, no factory, hospital or school can function.
whyWrong: Roads are one part of a much bigger system.
Buildings sit on infrastructure; they aren't it.
questions.action: List the infrastructure your school depends on.

questions.prompt: Why does Goal 9 combine industry, innovation and infrastructure?
options: They're unrelated but were left over
Each depends on the others — you can't run a factory without power or invent without labs
questions.whyCorrect: They're one system. Infrastructure lets industry exist, industry funds innovation, and innovation makes both cleaner and cheaper.
whyWrong: The three are tightly connected.
The grouping is about dependency, not spelling.
questions.action: Trace how electricity reaches one thing you used today.

questions.prompt: The world makes 17.3% more per person than in 2015, but emissions are up 8.3%. This means:
options: Production is growing faster than emissions, but emissions are still rising
questions.whyCorrect: Manufacturing is getting cleaner per unit made — but total output grew enough that emissions still hit a record. Efficiency alone isn't enough.
whyWrong: Emissions reached an all-time high in 2024.
Both figures moved substantially.
questions.action: Ask what 'cleaner per item' misses when you make more items.

questions.prompt: LDC manufacturing per person grew 40.6% while sub-Saharan Africa's fell 5.9%. This shows:
options: Different groupings can move in opposite directions — 'developing' is not one story
questions.whyCorrect: The LDC and sub-Saharan Africa groupings overlap but aren't identical — averages hide enormous variation between countries.
whyWrong: Both figures are correct for their groupings.
It's a crucial lesson about how averages mislead.
questions.action: Find two countries in the same region with very different economies.

questions.prompt: About what share of internationally traded goods travels by sea?
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly 80% by volume — 11.6 billion tons in 2023. Air freight is fast but tiny by weight; the world economy floats.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
Far too low — shipping dominates trade by volume.
questions.action: Track a container ship live on a marine traffic site.

questions.prompt: A country with 91 researchers per million mostly has to:
questions.whyCorrect: With almost no research capacity, countries import technology and pay for it — so the profits and the know-how stay abroad.
whyWrong: Technology gets imported, not skipped.
That requires research capacity it doesn't have.
questions.action: Ask why a country would want to invent things itself.

questions.prompt: The world's clean energy prevented 2.6 gigatons of CO2, yet 2024 set an emissions record. Why?
options: The clean energy figure is fake
Total energy demand grew faster than clean energy replaced it
questions.whyCorrect: Clean energy is being added on top of fossil fuels rather than replacing them, because total demand keeps climbing.
whyWrong: The avoided emissions are real and measured.
Clean energy reduces emissions; the problem is scale.
questions.action: Ask what 'adding' versus 'replacing' energy means.

questions.prompt: Small manufacturers matter to development because:
options: They employ most industrial workers in developing countries
questions.whyCorrect: Small firms are where most industrial jobs are — which is why 31% credit access is such a serious constraint on employment.
whyWrong: Large firms and informal trade dominate tax receipts.
Exports are dominated by large firms.
questions.action: Count the small businesses on one street near you.

questions.prompt: The 4G gap between low-income countries (52%) and the world (92%) is about:
questions.whyCorrect: A 40-point gap. Nearly half of low-income populations are stuck on older, slower networks — or none at all.
whyWrong: Ten times too small.
The gap is very large.
questions.action: Ask what you can do on 4G that you can't on 2G.

questions.prompt: R&D spending sits at 1.95% of GDP. The SDG aim is to:
options: Substantially increase it, especially in developing countries
questions.whyCorrect: Target 9.5 calls for more research spending and more researchers — particularly where capacity is lowest, like sub-Saharan Africa's 91 per million.
whyWrong: The goal is more research, not less.
Standing still leaves the research gap in place.
questions.action: Find out whether your country's research spending is rising.

questions.prompt: Developing countries went from 38% to 54% of sea freight since 2000. This mostly reflects:
options: More manufacturing and trade happening in developing economies
questions.whyCorrect: Factories moved. As Asia in particular industrialised, the goods — and the shipping — moved with them.
whyWrong: Total sea freight nearly doubled over this period.
Weather does not shift trade shares.
questions.action: Check where three items in your home were made.

questions.prompt: The single clearest sign that Goal 9 progress is uneven is:
options: 4% 5G coverage in low-income countries versus 51% globally
questions.whyCorrect: A 47-fold researcher gap and a 4%-versus-51% 5G gap say the same thing: new capability arrives where money already is.
whyWrong: Ship size says little about fairness.
That's a global structure figure, not an equity gap.
questions.action: Name one technology that reached everyone quickly and ask why.
